title: Solving large-scale open pit mining production scheduling problems by integer programming
contribution: Analyses a MILP for open pit mining production scheduling with block-level processing decisions (integrated cutoff grades) and makes it tractable: NP-hardness, existence and NP-hardness of per-period split ratios, and an integral precedence polytope, so that the Lagrangean dual equals the LP bound and is computed by a bundle method over min-cut subproblems in 3.6-17.5% of the LP time; LP-dual-based column aggregation ('binnings') loses under 0.06%, and greedy sub-MIP plus LNS heuristics reach 0.05% of the aggregated model's optimum on 29 BHP Billiton instances.
problem_entry: Published IP/MIP models for the OPMPSP fix cutoff grades a priori and treat scheduling units as homogeneous in ore; the model D-MIP (Froyland's; Boland et al. [6]) decides processing per block while mining stays at aggregate level, and the thesis asks whether its many extra variables can be afforded (pp. 5, 7, 25-32).
key_idea: Per period the processing variables solve a continuous bounded knapsack, so optimal processing follows one split ratio per period (a cutoff grade). Exact split ratios are NP-hard, but the LP duals of the processing rows are split ratios of the LP, so they define bins with a (1 ± ε) band. Relaxing the resource rows leaves an integral polytope whose Lagrangean subproblems are min-cuts (Möhring et al.). Greedy sub-MIPs over nested precedence-feasible index sets give start solutions (pp. 45-50, 55-63, 87-107).
assumptions: Binary monotone start variables, continuous mined and processed fractions, precedence via cumulative sums, one mining and one processing knapsack row per period, no general integers, SOS, indicators or big-M (p. 30); deterministic block model, known prices, fixed capacities, perfect grade control (p. 15); hidden assumption that a fractionally mined aggregate is mined uniformly, exposed by the author (p. 31); integer PCKP data for the hardness proofs (pp. 33, 48-49), b1 >= 0 for cuts (p. 64), m in Omega(K) (p. 61); 29 instances from three BHP Billiton mines (marvin 8513 blocks at three aggregations, wa 96821 blocks in 125 panels, ca 29266 blocks with 25 scenarios) (pp. 18-19).
proof_devices: NP-hardness of D-MIP and D-MIP' by reduction from the precedence-constrained knapsack problem, with node splitting for D-MIP (Prop. 2.1, pp. 37-38)
LP reduction by eliminating x or y without loss, a presolve step shown to preserve the resource multipliers (Prop. 3.1, Remark 3.3, pp. 43-44)
Split ratios from the split item of a continuous bounded knapsack (Prop. 3.4, pp. 45-46) and their interval computed from an optimal solution (Prop. 3.7, p. 47)

NP-hardness of computing split ratios: a PCKP containment test encoded in a one-period D-MIP' with an auxiliary aggregate and processing profits 1/2 and 1/3, then turned into a full PCKP algorithm (Prop. 3.9, pp. 48-50)
Integrality of the precedence polytope by a bijective substitution to cumulative variables (TU rows with one ±1 or a 1/-1 pair) plus a convex-combination argument for z (Prop. 3.10, pp. 51-52)

LD = LP via Geoffrion's integrality property (Prop. 3.11, p. 55); Lagrangean subproblem as unconstrained project scheduling solved by a minimum a-b-cut, converted to a K-cut in O(KT), total O(NT + mKT^2 log(K^2 T/m)) (Lemma 3.12, Prop. 3.13, Cor. 3.14, pp. 57-61)
LP duals of the processing rows are split ratios for every LP optimum, by complementary slackness (Prop. 3.15, p. 63)
Cuts with b1 >= 0 rewritten without x and dualised so the subproblem stays a min-cut; variable fixings from predecessor-cone tonnage imposed in the digraph (Lemma 3.17, Prop. 3.18, pp. 64-68)
Feasibility of every greedy sub-MIP by zero extension of the previous solution (Lemma 6.2, pp. 99-100)
Disaggregation by fixing the aggregated solution's integers and solving the remaining LP of D-MIP (p. 94)
experiments: Pentium 4 3 GHz, 2 GB, single thread; CPLEX 11.0, ConicBundle 0.2d, Pseudoflow 3.21, SCIP 1.05; 29 instances (pp. 19-20). LP baseline searched over primal/dual simplex and barrier on three formulations (p. 76); bundle times as min-max over windows of 10 consecutive bundle sizes (pp. 78-80); LD within relative 1e-6 of the LP bound in 3.6-17.5% of the LP time (Table 4.1, p. 81). Binnings: 1 h, then 2 threads for 5 h; time to 1% and 0.5% gap; loss vs B^block under 0.06% (Tables 5.1-5.2, pp. 93-95). Heuristics against the proven optimum of B-MIP(B^0.01): within 0.5% (start heuristics) and 0.05% (with LNS) (Tables 6.1-6.2, pp. 105, 108). Failures reported. No seeds, variability, significance tests or shifted geometric means; ca rows are arithmetic means over 25 scenarios; §6.3 SCIP runs reported without numbers (pp. 110-111).
positioning: Literature sorted by approach and criticised by assumption (a priori cutoff grades) rather than by performance (pp. 25-29, 39). Builds on Möhring et al. (min-cut for project scheduling), Geoffrion and Fisher (Lagrangean theory), Caccetta et al. (multipliers as cutoff grades), Litvinchev-Tsurkov and Zipkin (aggregation), Briant et al. (bundle vs column generation), Berthold, Fischetti-Lodi and Danna et al. (sub-MIP heuristics), and Fricke (cuts, time-based greedy). Geoffrion's advice is answered with Geoffrion's own exceptions (p. 55). Model and shared results credited to Froyland and to Boland et al. [6] (pp. 7, 18, 29, 116).
writing: Roadmap and Conclusion section per chapter; a contributions subsection marking what also appears in [6] (p. 18); model criticism raised by the author first and answered by argument and by the strict variant D-MIP' (pp. 31-32); numeric headlines in the body (<0.06%, 0.05%) with adjectives in abstract and conclusion (pp. 5, 94, 116); 'the author conducted' for experiments; untested expectations hedged as 'may be expected'; a surprising number explained in its caption (p. 95); one slip pairs the Ch. 4 times with the instances in reverse order (p. 81).
limits_future: Printed: barrier near-optimal only on 4/25 y-D-LP scenarios (p. 76); bundle stopped before target precision (p. 81); wa unsolvable without binning (p. 93); PIR-MIP slow and unfinished on marvin-1038 (p. 106); branching alone does not move the root bound (p. 111). Not measured: the precedence violation hidden in (2.5d) (p. 31), the never-binding mining rows (pp. 81-82), few aggregates (p. 109 fn. 3), gaps against the aggregated model's optimum (pp. 104-105). Future: dualised valid inequalities (e.g. SCIP c-MIR) in a Lagrangean branch-and-cut, or a different relaxation; faster PIR-MIP (pp. 106, 111-113, 117).

method_links.note: Baseline constructed by searching simplex and barrier over three equivalent LP formulations for the fastest route; both arms compute the same bound (LD = LP; relative objective at most 1.000001); the conventional simplex route is given in prose ('the result would be even clearer'). Differences from the Method: the baseline is strengthened rather than stripped, and only one factor is tabulated.

Steps 1 and 7: every limit printed where it arises, with a count or size (4/25 barrier failures, bundle precision, wa out of memory, PIR-MIP unfinished, root bound unmoved by branching), and a closing agenda. Step 4's import move appears as project-scheduling min-cut and pseudoflow brought into mine scheduling. No later closure visible in this text.

The approximate model produces and the faithful model decides: LP duals used only heuristically to form bins; the aggregated solution's integers fixed and the rest re-solved as an LP of the full D-MIP; losses measured in D-MIP. Same device as Method 5 step 3 and Method 1 step 2, applied to model aggregation rather than arithmetic (inferred analogy).
The heuristic premise that LP split ratios approximate MIP split ratios is checked against exact intervals from an optimal MIP solution on one instance: maximum relative deviation 8.3% (Fig. 5.1).

Two expectations left unmeasured although his own solutions could have counted them: the precedence violations hidden in (2.5d) 'may be expected to be minor', and D-MIP is expected to be easier than D-MIP'. Weak: a student work, and the beliefs concern model fidelity rather than solver behaviour.
Test set of 29 instances assembled with a stated purpose per subset, and its bias admitted later; no written admission rules, no availability statement, no independent solution checks.
Dual bounds presented as what gives engineers confidence in a plan (trust through a bound); no independent checker; a seed at most (inferred).

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: Pessimistic reporting of the method's own tuning parameter (min-max over a window)
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Bundle running times reported as the smallest of the per-window maxima over 10 consecutive maximum bundle sizes, because the dependence is volatile and the best size cannot be guaranteed; objective values reported the same way; multiplier deviations as the worst over all sizes.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: LP-analogue proxy for an NP-hard structural quantity, with a safety band and a measured loss
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Split ratios of D-MIP are NP-hard to compute (Prop. 3.9), but the LP duals of the processing rows are split ratios of D-LP (Prop. 3.15); bins are built around (1 ± ε)π_t; the proxy is compared with exact intervals on one instance (8.3%); the loss is under 0.06% before LP disaggregation and smaller after it.

transferable: Search the baseline before comparing: run every LP algorithm (primal, dual, barrier with and without crossover) on every equivalent formulation, compare against the fastest route found, and give the conventional route in a sentence (p. 76; Table 4.1, p. 81).

Report a tuning parameter of your own method pessimistically: over windows of 10 consecutive values take each window's worst time and report the best window; report accuracy deviations as the worst over all values (pp. 78-80).

Replace an NP-hard structural parameter by its LP counterpart from the duals, keep a (1 ± ε) band unaggregated, check the proxy against exact values on one solvable instance, and measure the loss in the full model (pp. 63, 91-95).
Disaggregate an aggregated MIP solution by fixing its integer variables in the full model and solving the remaining LP; tabulate the gain over fixed-weight disaggregation (pp. 94-95).

Keep a Lagrangean min-cut subproblem intact when adding cuts: rewrite each cut without the variables that break the network (b1 >= 0, Lemma 3.17), dualise it, and impose variable fixings in the graph (pp. 64-68).

Build start heuristics as nested precedence-feasible index sets solved as sub-MIPs; prove once by zero extension (Lemma 6.2) that every step is feasible; keep the not-yet-added columns LP-relaxed instead of deleting them, for a global view (pp. 98-103).
Confirm a diagnosis about a custom tree search with a control run of the stock solver, here SCIP defaults with the separators off (p. 111).
When a model critique is likely, raise it yourself, offer the strict variant, and prove how the two relate (D-MIP is a relaxation of D-MIP' with the same LP bound) (pp. 31-32, 44).
State each gap's formula and denominator in the table caption, and name which optimum it is measured against (pp. 105, 108).
coauthors: None: a single-author Diplomarbeit, supervised by Rolf H. Möhring (p. 3). The model is credited to Gary Froyland and to Boland, Dumitrescu, Froyland and Gleixner [6]; Marco Lübbecke guided the layout; Tobias Achterberg, Timo Berthold and Kati Wolter introduced him to SCIP (pp. 7, 29).

quotes.text: The main goal was to determine the fastest way for solving the LP-relaxation in practise using any of the solvers and formulations from Section 3.1, in order to compare this with the performance of the lagrangean approach.
Rather it seems fair to select a range of maximum bundle sizes where the algorithm works well and take the worst value found in this range.
